analysis.headline: Passed the House 231-199 on July 18, 2019; the Senate read it twice, placed it on its calendar, and never voted before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Raise the Wage Act would have raised the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $7.25 to $15.00 an hour over seven years, and after that automatically adjusted it each year to match the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees [S5]. It would also have phased out the lower, separate minimum wages for tipped workers, for newly hired workers under 20, and for workers with disabilities under special certificates, eventually paying all of them the same minimum wage as everyone else [S2][S4][S5]. The Labor Department would have had to publish each increase 60 days before it took effect so employers could plan [S2][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, whose hourly pay would have more than doubled over seven years; tipped workers, whose employers could currently pay as little as $2.13 in cash wages before tips; newly hired workers under 20, who could be paid $4.25 for their first 90 days; and workers with disabilities who held special certificates allowing subminimum pay, all of whom would eventually have been entitled to the full minimum wage [S2][S4][S5].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in defined annual steps — $8.40, $9.50, $10.60, $11.70, $12.80, $13.90, then $15.00 — starting in the third month after enactment, a direct pay raise for anyone at the bottom of the wage scale.
After reaching $15, the wage would rise each year by the percentage increase in the national median hourly wage, so it would stop losing value to inflation between congressional updates.

Phases out the tipped minimum wage by raising the required cash wage by up to $1.50 a year until it reaches the full minimum wage, so servers' base pay would no longer depend on tips covering the gap.

Phases out the $4.25 training wage for newly hired workers under 20 and the special certificates that let employers pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage, with the Department of Labor required to offer transition assistance to employers and referral information to affected workers.

Requires the Department of Labor to publish every increase in the Federal Register and on its website 60 days before it takes effect, and directs the Government Accountability Office to report on the effects of the first increases on businesses, including small businesses.

analysis.who_pays: The employers of low-wage workers would bear the cost directly: restaurants, hotels, retail, and other businesses that pay minimum wage, plus businesses built around the tipped-employee and subminimum-wage systems, whose required cash labor costs would have risen steadily for six to seven years until every covered worker reached the full minimum wage [S5]. A Republican motion to add an exemption for very small businesses — those employing fewer than 10 people with under $1 million in annual sales — failed 210-218, so no such carve-out was included [S7][S8].

drawbacks.text: The bill would have roughly doubled required hourly labor costs for minimum-wage employers over seven years, a real cost for small restaurants and retailers; an amendment offered through a motion to recommit would have exempted enterprises with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in annual sales, and it failed 210-218, leaving no small-business exemption in the version that passed.

Phasing out the separate lower wage for newly hired workers under 20 removes the discounted rate employers could use to take a chance on inexperienced teenagers, which opponents argued could reduce first-job opportunities for young workers.

Eliminating special subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities would end arrangements under which some disabled workers were legally paid below minimum wage; the bill's answer was a scheduled phase-in plus transition assistance that the Department of Labor must provide only 'upon request,' and critics of ending the program worried about the continuing employment of workers in those settings.

Because the wage floor would automatically rise each year with median wage growth after reaching $15, future Congresses would lose the chance to pause or recalibrate increases during a downturn — the bill itself directs Congress to assess GAO findings and consider 'actions to delay the next scheduled wage increases,' an implicit acknowledgment that the schedule might need adjusting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for the workers covered: a guaranteed schedule taking the federal minimum from $7.25 to $15.00, plus equal treatment for tipped, teenage, and disabled workers who were previously legally paid less [S5]. The costs fall on identifiable employers, and the strongest good-faith concerns — strain on very small businesses and the effect of ending subminimum-wage certificates on employment for workers with disabilities — were addressed in the bill only with a long phase-in and optional assistance rather than exemptions, and the small-business exemption offered on the floor was voted down 210-218 [S7][S8]. The design is a deliberate policy bet that broad wage gains outweigh the risks of phasing in higher labor costs over seven years, with GAO reporting built in as a check; it is not a narrowly targeted tweak, which is also why opposition from affected employers was solid.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 231-199, the Senate placed it on its calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019, and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced January 16, 2019 by Rep. Bobby Scott and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The committee marked it up on March 6, 2019, ordering it reported 28-20, and reported it amended on July 11, 2019 with House Report 116-150.

Under a rule from the Rules Committee, the House debated the bill on July 18, 2019; a motion to recommit with instructions to add a small-business exemption for firms with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales failed 210-218 (Roll no. 495), with 195 of 199 Republicans in favor and 14 Democrats crossing over.
The House passed the bill 231-199 (Roll no. 496) — 228 Democrats and 3 Republicans in favor, 192 Republicans, 6 Democrats, and 1 Independent opposed.

The Senate received the bill on July 18, 2019, read it a second time on July 22, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 156); no further action was taken for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

key_actors.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
key_actors.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 582 on January 16, 2019 and guided it through his committee, which reported it to the House on July 11, 2019, by a 28-20 vote.

key_actors.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
key_actors.what_they_did: Held a markup on March 6, 2019, ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute 28-20, and reported it amended (H. Rept. 116-150).

key_actors.name: Members of the House of Representatives
key_actors.what_they_did: Rejected the Meuser motion to recommit with a small-business exemption 210-218, then passed the bill 231-199, with 6 Democrats and 1 Independent voting against and 3 Republicans in favor.

key_actors.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
key_actors.what_they_did: The Senate under his leadership received the bill on July 18, 2019 and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019, where it stayed; the Senate never brought it to a vote for the rest of the Congress.

key_actors.name: Rep. Dan Meuser
key_actors.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a small-business exemption covering enterprises with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in annual sales; the motion failed 210-218.
